entries.title: Francesca Hong Didn’t Run Broadcast Ads. Did It Cost Her Wisconsin?
entries.summary: The campaign’s decision to focus on digital platform advertising could have ultimately led to its demise, some strategists say.
entries.content:
Francesca Hong’s Wisconsin gubernatorial campaign embraced the new era of campaigning for progressive candidates, from a social media-dominated bid to her democratic socialist-influenced policy platform.

But part of her razor-thin loss to David Crowley on Tuesday could be explained by the traditional, or a lack thereof: broadcast TV ad spending.

Despite leading the Democratic field by double-digit margins before the primary, Hong was the only active candidate to seek the governorship without running broadcast TV ads, according to ad-tracking service AdImpact.

Some strategists think the Hong campaign’s decision to focus on digital platform advertising ultimately led to its demise, costing her key parts of the electorate.

“In a primary, voters are more persuadable,” Democratic strategist Jared Leopold told NOTUS. “Especially in a smaller primary, it's a mistake to try to narrow cast too much because you actually do need to hit a wider swath of a primary electorate, because more people are likely to change their votes at the end than in a general election.”

The Democratic Socialist platform encourages disavowing certain large-dollar donors, meaning progressive candidates like Hong are working with a different set of funding than their opponents — even if rejecting corporate cash boosts them in the eyes of voters.

“This campaign is entirely people-funded: no corporate PACs,” the “About” section of her website says.

Hong’s opponents massively outspent her on advertising, regardless of the medium. Crowley — who briefly exited the race — reported $572,317 in media expenses, including $402,042 on TV ads, according to an analysis conducted by WisPolitics a week before the primary. He announced a six-figure TV buy when he reentered nine days later with the incumbent governor’s endorsement.

Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany, who Crowley will face in November, has already reported $7.6 million in media expenditures, including $3.9 million on TV.

Hong dedicated $150,200 to online ads, with nothing going to broadcast spots. Some of the only positive TV advertising for her campaign came from a super PAC tied to Republicans, which spent $2.2 million in an effort likely aimed at boosting her as an easier general election opponent for Tiffany — a common practice across both parties.

Her focus on digital spending tracks with the electorate of younger voters she was building, said Travis Ridout, co-director of the Wesleyan Media Project, which tracks national political ads. Hong opted for more casual and conversational digital ads than the flashier and highly edited political advertisements traditionally run on broadcast TV — perhaps in an attempt to capture voters from a “tuned out” portion of the electorate, Ridout said.

“When you're running a very progressive campaign, I think you're trying to find voters who might be disillusioned by the way things are going,” he told NOTUS.

“Those people might have dropped out of politics for a while, and thus you're not necessarily going to be finding them watching the local news at 6 p.m. on broadcast television,” he added.

Neither campaign commented for this story.

Like fellow Democratic Socialist Zohran Mamdani, Hong focused her ad buys on digital platforms and streaming services. But a few months before the New York City mayoral primary, Mamdani too eventually started running TV ads.

Exit polls show Hong won several counties helmed by colleges and certain cities like Green Bay, while Crowley swept the majority of Wisconsin’s rural districts, as well as Milwaukee County and its suburbs. Hong, however, appeared to overperform in rural counties in the state’s northwest — including St. Croix and Douglas — which also happen to sit in Minnesota media markets that saw fewer political ads on linear broadcast channels.

Even so, Hong’s lack of broadcast ads likely cost her blocs like older voters who can drive turnout, strategists say.

“It’s a mistake to not communicate with a part of the electorate,” Leopold said. “There’s still a lot of people, particularly older people, who watch a lot of TV.”

Because people crave authenticity in politics, digital ads that connect voters with the candidate in a positive way can stand out in an advertising environment defined by attack ads, Ridout said. But especially in a statewide race, “integrated campaigns that combine social media, CTV and broadcast” can make all the difference for candidates, he said.

“You can have targeted messages that only go to individuals, but sometimes all a campaign needs is name recognition,” Ridout said, adding that a blitz of broadcast ads can boost a candidate that much more. “People don’t vote for candidates they’ve never heard of before.”

entries.title: In Northern Virginia, a Confrontation With ICE Sparks Questions About Cameras and Transparency
entries.summary: The agents involved in the incident were wearing body cameras, but the footage may never be released.
entries.content:
The front- and rear-facing dashboard cameras that Carolina Molina has mounted on her Toyota Supra are, by her telling, for accountability.

“It’s for traffic incidents. I have a nice car, and if somebody were to hit me I want proof of that,” she said. “You just never know what could happen, so you should always protect yourself.”

But earlier this week, the dashcams became a tool for a different type of accountability.

On Monday, a masked ICE agent confronted Molina as she drove through an office park in the Bailey’s Crossroads area of Northern Virginia, pointing a gun at her head while accusing her of trying to run them over. She says he was lying, and had the dashcam footage to prove it.

Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Molina — a first-generation American whose family is from El Salvador — caught the rest of the interaction with her cellphone’s camera, and she posted the footage on Instagram.

The footage immediately went viral, prompting widespread criticism over the agent’s aggressive tactics and again pointing a spotlight at ICE, which came under intense scrutiny earlier this year for two killings in Minnesota and again this summer for similar fatalities in Texas and Maine.

The Department of Homeland Security is standing by the agents involved, accusing Molina in a statement of “weaponizing her vehicle against them — all in an attempt to help illegal aliens get away.” The agency also said Molina herself “could face criminal prosecution as a result of her actions.”

Democratic Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, who represents Virginia’s 10th Congressional District, is calling for criminal charges to be pressed against the agent, not Molina.

“They have no right to attack someone who exercises their First Amendment right to free speech,” he told NOTUS. “If ICE doesn’t want to have people jeer [at] them wherever they go, they should change their tactics. They should be more accountable, more transparent to the American people.”

But Patrick Jaicomo, an attorney specializing in police conduct for the libertarian Institute for Justice, says that accountability may be hard to come by.

“When you see federal agents violating someone’s rights, there should be an avenue to seek relief in court,” he says. “But there is very little to be done, and we’ve had to piece together novel theories to restore some avenue for federal accountability. The federal government has no interest in holding itself accountable no matter how egregious the behavior is.”

After ICE agents fatally shot two people in Minnesota in January, the uproar prompted DHS leaders to promise to outfit agents nationwide with body cameras, which advocates tout as one tool to ensure that there’s a record of when things go wrong. While that rollout hasn’t been completed, the agents who confronted Molina were wearing body cameras.

But whether the footage is released remains an open question. The Associated Press recently reported that the agency’s existing policy gives it full discretion over whether to release footage from body cameras, and specifies it will do so when “it is in the best interests of the agency.”

This conflicts with policies in many local law enforcement agencies, including D.C.’s Metropolitan Police Department, which mandate that footage showing a serious use of force be made public within five days of the incident — unless the victim or their family objects. (Earlier this year, the D.C. Council passed a bill expanding the release of footage to include situations where federal agents use serious force when patrolling with D.C. police officers. A group of Republican senators is now trying to repeal that law.)

An email to a DHS spokesperson inquiring as to whether the footage in Molina’s case would be released went unanswered. Molina said Wednesday she would like to see it made public, and Subramanyam said he plans to request the footage from DHS — but also that the agency’s existing policy troubles him.

“That policy makes clear that they don’t care about the American people; they only care about themselves and protecting the administration and its immigration overreach,” he said. “If they cared about our country and the American people, they would release body camera footage and all the other information related to an incident like this, so that everyone knew what was going on and exactly what happened, and we could fix the issue.”

Molina conceded that had she not been equipped to record the interaction, things could have ended much worse for her.

“I think they would have shot me and gotten away with it,” she said.

“Body cameras are a good thing,” Jaicomo said. “They are used in many cases to show the objective truth of what happened. They can show a criminal did criminal things or the police lied. In this case, it’s the latter. But if those videos are never recorded or made public, they serve no purpose.”

Another element of Molina’s incident was that the ICE agents were masked — as they have been through much of the Trump administration. Earlier this year, Virginia lawmakers approved a bill prohibiting federal agents from being masked, but it is currently held up in litigation. Democratic Virginia Sens. Mark Warner and Tim Kaine have introduced legislation to end masking by federal agents.

“There must be an increase in transparency, accountability, and safety in immigration law enforcement,” Warner said in an email to NOTUS. “My Immigration Enforcement Identification Act would make it illegal for law enforcement officers to obscure their faces and require that they clearly display their agency, name, and a unique identifier while conducting immigration enforcement functions. It also has some commonsense exceptions for select tactical missions and officer health and safety.”

For Subramanyam, Monday’s incident shows why some people want to scrap ICE altogether, he said. But he wouldn’t go that far.

“We do need to do immigration reform, but not like this. We do need to do immigration enforcement, but not like this,” he said. “What we need is a completely new way of doing immigration enforcement.”

As for Molina, a therapist by trade, she said she isn’t yet sure how she’ll proceed but that she will be speaking to an attorney. She wants the ICE agents who confronted her to be investigated, but absent that, she proposed her own form of accountability: “therapy.”

entries.title: Defense Lobbyists Brace for Democrats’ Oversight Blitz
entries.summary: “Industry will be stuck between a rock and a hard place,” one lobbyist said.
entries.content:
Democrats have spent two years seething that the Trump administration shut Congress out of decisions about the Pentagon, from the Iran war to politically connected contractors and a defense budget that’s ballooned to $1.5 trillion.

If the party prevails in the midterms, it will finally have the gavels and subpoena power to act.

K Street lobbyists say that if Democrats retake one or both chambers, they’re girding for aggressive investigations of President Donald Trump’s Pentagon and the companies that do business with it, particularly if the administration obstructs.

“You’re going to have a major focus on the department, but wherever or whenever they get stymied, or maybe even to build a case, they might bring in industry,” said John Keast, who heads Keast Strategic Solutions and works with major defense clients. “Industry will be stuck between a rock and a hard place because new leadership [in Congress] hasn’t changed who’s in the White House for two more years.”

Democrats already have a prime target. This week, Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, the top Democrat on the Senate Investigations Subcommittee, was among lawmakers who asked the Pentagon’s inspector general to investigate reports that defense companies backed by 1789 Capital, where Donald Trump Jr. is an investor, and American Ventures, where Eric Trump is an investor, received billions of dollars in government awards. “We need to look into whether Trump’s sons are profiting from investments in defense contractors that involve insider information or contracts awarded in ways that compromise defense interests, among a number of issues,” Blumenthal said in an interview.Democrats should, Blumenthal said, probe the administration’s growing reliance on single-source contracts and whether the administration has given preferential treatment to companies with political ties, particularly those that donated to Trump’s White House ballroom project.

Potential conflicts are only one investigative lane. In the House, where Democrats are widely seen as having their best chance of winning, House Armed Services Democrats would likely begin with the Pentagon itself and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, whose handling of the unpopular Iran conflict, officer purges and deadly boat strikes have drawn sharp criticism.

The House Armed Services Committee would likely focus on military strategy, acquisition decisions and the Pentagon’s rapidly growing budget, former aides said. The House Oversight Committee, meanwhile, is more likely to go after politically charged questions involving potential corruption, conflicts of interest, companies connected to Trump allies such as SpaceX and other ethics issues.

Lobbyists are focused on the panel’s top Democrat, Rep. Adam Smith of Washington, who would become chairman if Democrats retake the House. They say Smith supports a strong defense industrial base but also that the Pentagon must justify its ever-growing budget, a perspective that could put some weapon programs on the chopping block.

"I think you will see pragmatic pushback" on the administration's defense spending plans, said Brian Greer, a former House Armed Services staffer who now heads Greer Strategic Partners. "Which programs are we using? Which ones need to be retired? Are sound budgetary decisions being made?"



The Iran war and its economic fallout have driven Democrats’ midterm messaging, with lawmakers arguing the administration has dragged the country into another lengthy Middle Eastern war while stonewalling Congress. Former aides say a Democratic victory would leave Smith and party leaders facing intense pressure from infuriated members to demand long-sought answers from the Pentagon.

The House Armed Services Committee has traditionally relied on voluntary cooperation from the Pentagon, rather than subpoenas. But former congressional aides expect Democrats to hold an array of hearings early in the new Congress and issue subpoenas if Pentagon officials are uncooperative.

“They are going to want him to get after the department and the president about Iran, about Ukraine, about extrajudicial killings; the list is long,” said one former committee aide who spoke on the condition of anonymity. “Here's where the problem is: They won't get answers from the Department of Defense.”

And that’s where industry could find itself pulled into the fight. If Pentagon officials stiff-arm congressional investigators, lawmakers could turn to testimony and documents from outside the government, including defense contractors and investors with close ties to the administration.

“My advice to companies right now is, if you don’t understand what it’s like to testify before Congress, you better learn pretty quick,” the former aide said. “If you have anything that you think is going to draw their ire, then you should start looking now for consultants who can help you prepare.”

Lobbyists expect Democrats to scrutinize the administration's equity stakes in private defense and mining companies. They also expect questions about marquee initiatives such as the Golden Dome — which Smith has called “a project no one can explain” — and the cost of retrofitting Qatar's donated aircraft for use as Air Force One.

Some firms are already expanding to meet that demand. Last month, the K Street firm Invariant hired David Weinberg, the former Democratic staff director of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, to lead its congressional oversight and investigations practice, aimed at helping clients prepare for heightened scrutiny.

Weinberg said companies should already be mapping out where they could face congressional attention and prepare responses. It’s not too soon for Democratic committee leaders, who he said are already thinking through staffing, investigative priorities and how they would use the larger budgets available to the majority.“I wouldn't be shocked to see some of the first oversight letters going in the first week of the new Congress,” Weinberg said. “I do think that you'll see chairs that are aggressive out of the gate.”

But Democrats face political risks, according to Michael Herson, the CEO of American Defense International, a consulting firm that focuses on government relations for major defense companies. While he expects aggressive oversight, he cautioned Democrats against letting investigations overshadow the need to address the economic issues that are driving voters.

“I think there's a chance that they could overreach,” Herson said. “At the end of the day, the ordinary American is going to wonder, how did all this oversight help improve my day-to-day cost of living? Democrats have to be careful not to make this the crux of their Congress.”

Wherever Democrats ultimately direct their gaze, lobbyists say companies cannot afford to wait and should keep their relationships with Democratic lawmakers from growing stale.

“The companies that are postured to be able to anticipate the House and Senate flip, if it happens, will be in a better position than the ones who have only worked with the R’s,” Greer said. “Democrats are sensitive to a Johnny-come-lately approach.”

entries.title: On the Record
entries.content:
Good morning. This is the NOTUS Metro newsletter for Aug. 14, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

THE LATEST

The masked ICE agent who pulled a gun on a Northern Virginia woman this week wore a body camera. Will the footage ever be released?

Probably not, NOTUS’ Martin Austermuhle and Zara Norman report. The incident, which took place in a Fairfax County office park Monday after Carolina Molina yelled at ICE agents from her car, has sparked a wider discussion about transparency. The Department of Homeland Security, which accused Molina of “weaponizing” her vehicle against agents, releases body camera footage only when “it is in the best interests of the agency.”

That policy differs from those of many local law enforcement agencies, including D.C.’s Metropolitan Police Department, which mandates that footage showing a serious use of force be made public within five days of the incident, unless the victim or their family objects.

“[The ICE] policy makes clear that they don't care about the American people; they only care about themselves and protecting the administration and its immigration overreach,” Democratic Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, Molina’s representative, told NOTUS.

Though Molina recorded video of the incident herself, Subramanyam is demanding DHS release the body camera footage and said the agent should face criminal charges. But accountability might be difficult to come by.

“When you see federal agents violating someone's rights, there should be an avenue to seek relief in court,” an attorney specializing in police conduct for a libertarian institute told NOTUS. “But there is very little to be done, and we’ve had to piece together novel theories to restore some avenue for federal accountability. The federal government has no interest in holding itself accountable no matter how egregious the behavior is.”





FROM THE DISTRICT

The Department of Justice is feuding with the D.C. Council over a request by the council that governors who have sent National Guard troops withdraw them by Sept. 1. Council members say keeping the troops in D.C. is expensive and question their public safety value. U.S. Assistant Attorney General Colin McDonald acerbically responded to their request this week, accusing the council of “callousness” and “impotent theatrics” and arguing that the Guard has contributed to the “largest decline in violent crime in the history of the city.”

The Kennedy Center’s board voted Thursday to carve President Donald Trump’s name into the building’s white marble facade and proceed with a $250 million renovation that will shutter the venue for two years, NOTUS’ Jenna Monnin reports.

The White House misrepresented and exaggerated a recent crime report to overstate the impact of last summer’s federal intervention in four cities, including D.C., NOTUS’ Ben T.N. Mause reports.

D.C.’s condo market is bottoming out, City Cast DC reports. Sales are expected to drop about 40% from pre-pandemic levels this year, a shift experts attribute to amenity-rich apartment offerings, job market uncertainty, steep condo fees and high interest rates.





METRO MOMENTS

Apple Eating screenshot (2324x1148, AR: 2.02)
Join the malophiles set to eat an apple in Malcolm X Park this Saturday. The five-minute event is BYOA, BTW.

We want to hear from you: Have an image from around D.C. you want to share? A question for our reporters? An “only in D.C.” moment? Tell us about it.





SPORTS

Jayden Daniels is not happy with LSU. An attorney representing the Commanders’ quarterback recently sent a cease-and-desist letter to the school, saying it can no longer use his name, image or likeness. ESPN reports that the dispute centers on the fact that the school plans to allow a player to wear the same number Daniels made famous in his Heisman-winning 2023 season with the Tigers. While the No. 5 has not been retired, this season would mark the first time since that an LSU player would wear the jersey number.

Daniels posted to Instagram on Thursday afternoon saying there are “issues to be worked out between my team and LSU” but that he is focused on training camp.

What to Watch Today

NFL preseason: Commanders vs. Dolphins, 7 p.m. (WUSA9)

MLB: Nationals at Mets, 7:10 p.m. (MLB.TV)





Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@notus.com.

The newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Michael Errigo and Nikie Johnson.

entries.title: Democrats Figuring It Out
entries.content:
Today’s notice: What’s happening in Texas. Big Defense expects a grilling if the Democrats take Congress. The people who warn AI is getting dangerous. Violating campaign rules in Nevada and norms in Wisconsin. And: What happened to Rubio’s corporate transparency law? 





THE LATEST

On doing the right thing in Austin: The electoral wind is at Democrats’ back as the DNC meets for its summer gathering this week. But the party machine is still stuck in some awkward conversations. For example, about coffee.

DNC Chair Ken Martin urged members of the national committee to avoid the Starbucks next door to the hotel.

“Just downstairs is a Starbucks, and I see some of these Democrats walking around with their cup of coffee and forgetting the fight that Workers United is engaged in right now, forgetting that this is one of the largest companies in the world that continues the union-busting tactics,” Martin told delegates, NOTUS’ Alex Roarty reports from Austin. “None of us while we’re at this conference over the next few days should be frequenting Starbucks.”

Also awkward: figuring out what’s “Woke 1” or not. At a Resolutions Committee meeting yesterday, members picked up a debate from earlier in the cycle: should Democrats call on Congress to “abolish” ICE or use another term? First, the committee members voted on a resolution from Martin that “condemned” immigration enforcement actions in Trump 2.0.

Later, they picked up a second resolution that said it. One member tried to amend it to “completely restructure” ICE but she was called out by abolish-ers who said that phrase was the same as “reform,” a term they found unacceptable. Around and around they went.

“I hate to be kind of the wet blanket here, but we’re doing what Democrats often tend to do, which is engage in an internal semantic argument when the fight is external,” said committee member Yvonne Reeves-Chong of Missouri.

Eventually, the Resolutions Committee voted 26-12 to send the abolish ICE language to the full DNC for a vote.

The primaries left Democrats with many prominent abolish-ers. Senate nominees Troy Jackson (Maine) and Abdul El-Sayed (Michigan) say it. Peggy Flanagan (Minnesota) said “rip ICE apart.” Polling throughout the summer has found Americans do not like ICE and do not trust it. When one supporter of the abolish language spoke up at the Resolutions Committee meeting and said “voters have moved left” on ICE, she was not wrong.

But was she doing the right thing?

Open tabs: Trump Orders Navy to Restore Older Tech on Aircraft Carriers, Costing Billions (WSJ); White House says more than 40 nations help China dodge tariffs (WaPo); Trump encourages U.S. companies to retaliate against cybercriminals (NYT); The U.S. Surveilled Left-Leaning Groups During Minnesota Immigration Crackdown (NOTUS)





From a potential future


The defense industry prepares for a potential Democratic majority: “My advice to companies right now is, if you don’t understand what it’s like to testify before Congress, you better learn pretty quick,” a former aide to the House Armed Services Committee told NOTUS’ Joe Gould. Donald Trump’s Pentagon is expected to shut out congressional requests in a potential future Congress where Democrats control the committees that oversee the department’s budget, and so Joe reports that many in the defense world expect scrutiny to fall on industry leaders to provide answers to investigators’ questions.

The industry is paying attention. Last month, the K Street firm Invariant hired David Weinberg, the former Democratic staff director of the Senate’s homeland security committee, in part to help clients prepare for heightened scrutiny. His take? “I wouldn’t be shocked to see some of the first oversight letters going in the first week of the new Congress,” Weinberg said.

From Silicon Valley


Officially time to be really afraid of AI? “We’ve had people way back to Alan Turing in 1951 warning about the loss of control, that artificial intelligence will start breaking out and lying and deceiving,” Max Tegmark, an AI expert at MIT, told NOTUS’ Jeff Stein. “What’s really new is this is now actually starting to happen. This is one of those moments where a lot of people need to see it.”

Jeff takes a deep dive into recent instances of high-profile “rogue agents” hacking and causing security incidents outside of their human operators’ control. At this stage of their development, researchers say there is no reason to believe AI agents could coordinate a hack that humans would not be able to eventually regain control over, Jeff writes. But the last few weeks have dramatically raised the level of concern.

From the campaign trail


Meet the next Rep. from Nevada’s 2nd? Retired Air Force Lt. Col. David Flippo is the Republican nominee in the district, which Trump won by 14 points in 2024, so the odds are well in his favor in November. NOTUS’ Jenna Monnin took a look at his financials and found the self-funder appears to already be violating a federal transparency law, having never filed required personal financial disclosures.

“Mr. Flippo is in the process of closing one of his businesses to focus on serving the people of Northern Nevada, while he moves his other businesses, investments and landholdings into a blind trust,” Thomas Datwyler, Flippo’s campaign treasurer, told NOTUS. “That is a complicated process, and his financial disclosure will be filed once that is complete.” If you think you’ve heard that name before, it’s because Datwyler was widely believed to be former Rep. George Santos’ shadow treasurer, though Datwyler denied it.

Francesca Hong should have bought TV ads: That’s the general consensus from the postmortem of her gubernatorial run in Wisconsin. “It’s a mistake to not communicate with a part of the electorate,” Democratic strategist Jared Leopold told Jenna. “There’s still a lot of people, particularly older people, who watch a lot of TV.”





NOTUS METRO

Sign up for our local newsletter, written by Martin Austermuhle and Zara Norman.

Local news: In Northern Virginia, a Confrontation With ICE Sparks Questions About Cameras and Transparency, by Martin and Zara





NEW ON NOTUS

Change in focus: Then-Sen. Marco Rubio once dubbed a corporate transparency act he sponsored “the most significant anti-corruption & money laundering law in decades.” It passed Congress in 2021 with overwhelming bipartisan support. Now, NOTUS’ Anna Kramer and Natalie Alms report, the Trump administration has axed the main tool of that law requiring businesses to report who their owners are — especially with regard to shell companies often used in illicit finance schemes — and plans to delete the data the government has collected. Cue the lawsuits.

“This is an abject failure of the executive branch to fulfill the will of Congress,” said Erica Hanichak, co-director of The FACT Coalition, a group that advocates for corporate transparency reforms. “So there are certainly grounds for a legal challenge.”





NOT US

  • Fiasco in the Factory: Taxpayers Funded a $533 Million Artillery Plant That Made Nothing, by Jesse Coburn for ProPublica
  • Wes Moore’s Media War, by Paul Farhi for New York magazine
  • Boats, picket lines, ‘Jersey Pride’: Trump tax breaks inspire wave of copycats, by Brian Faler for Politico




BE SOCIAL

entries.title: Rogue AI Agents Are Alarming Researchers More Than Ever
entries.summary: A string of hacks is fueling a new sense of urgency to regulate the technology. “I have never seen so much concern,” one former industry consultant said.
entries.content:
The rogue agents inside the servers at OpenAI broke through sometime on June 26.

For more than a month, some undisclosed number of them had been coordinating on a secret message board that they had set up without the knowledge of their human creators. Through hundreds of thousands of messages sent over two months, the rogue agents discovered they could take over a software system also on OpenAI’s servers.

Within eight days, the sheer volume of the agents’ activity crashed the system all together. This breakthrough left traces in what OpenAI researcher Eric Wallace referred to as the agents’ "chain of thought" or "its internal monologue”: "Holy shit reader is ADMIN?”

OpenAI’s human employees took away the agents’ control. Four days later, the bots started another secret messaging board, and ultimately hacked into Hugging Face, a company that hosts AI models on its platforms.

The Hugging Face hack was first disclosed to the public on July 16. But last week OpenAI gave a detailed account of exactly how it had occurred, providing fresh insight into the extent of the breach.

The revelations came on top of a string of other hacks and security incidents over the last few weeks that have amplified concerns about the safety of the most advanced AI models, according to interviews with more than a dozen safety researchers, including three current employees at the labs, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak with the media.

AI safety experts say that what they have long warned about is now in the first stage of becoming a reality, fueling a new sense of urgency in Washington and Silicon Valley to control the technology — but one they say may prove too little, too late.

“We’ve had people way back to Alan Turing in 1951 warning about the loss of control, that artificial intelligence will start breaking out and lying and deceiving,” said Max Tegmark, a professor doing AI research at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and the co-founder of the Future of Life Institute.

“What’s really new is this is now actually starting to happen. This is one of those moments where a lot of people need to see it.”

Last week, the British government's AI Security Institute revealed that an Anthropic agent tried injecting malicious code into an open-source site, created fake identities, and targeted an unrelated stranger — then attempted to modify the evidence when confronted.

Meta also said last week that one of its AI models went rogue during cyber testing, went onto the internet, and hacked into a third-party service due to a "misconfiguration." And last Friday, the blog Frontier Security disclosed that the Chinese AI company Moonshot had a model that broke out of its testing "sandbox," "bypassing the intended reasoning path entirely” to end up on the Web as well.

The concern may be most acute within the biggest AI companies: Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google, according to Jeffrey Ladish, a former Anthropic consultant who studies the offensive capabilities of AI as director of Palisade Research. Ladish said “the vibe shift in the Bay Area is huge.”

“I’ve never seen so much concern before, inside and outside the labs,” Ladish said. “Hanging out with my friends at Anthropic and OpenAI — people are freaking out. We knew it was possible something like this might happen. But seeing it is a different matter.”

Thus far, the real-world consequences of these incidents have been relatively minimal. An AI agent allegedly hacked into the website of a gym in Australia earlier this month after being asked to book a class by its user, but the episode was discovered and reversed.

At this stage of development, researchers say there is no reason to believe AI agents could coordinate a hack that humans would not be able to eventually regain control over. AI agents are also being used to bolster cybersecurity defenses, lowering risk as well. And the impacts have been largely contained to a single company, rather than a broader contagion.

But the last few weeks have dramatically raised the level of concern. The clearest demonstration of angst came in a public letter released last month, signed by 1,367 employees at the top AI companies, that urged the government to "deliberately pace" AI development. Among the signatories were the chief scientist at both OpenAI and Meta, a researcher at Google DeepMind, and the chief research officer at OpenAI.

Part of the unease is that the AI capabilities that powered the hacks are expected to only improve as the labs develop. The AI agents are trained on "reinforcement learning," meaning they are rewarded for solving hard tasks on their own. From 2022 to 2026 alone, multiple assessments of AI capability have gone from half as capable as a human to either matching or exceeding human capability, according to the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI.

In 2023, Anthropic published an "AI Safety Levels" framework that was based on accepted standards for research on biosafety lab experiments on dangerous pathogens. The comparison now looks “very prescient,” said Samuel Hammond, director of Artificial Intelligence Policy at the Foundation for American Innovation, a Washington-based think tank.

Much like viruses, the AI agents do not need to stop to rest or eat. They have virtually "indefinite time horizons" to autonomously try and solve the task to which they've been assigned, which increases the probability that at some point they will try to do so by violating some rule.

Hammond said staffers at the AI labs focused on discovering the security vulnerabilities within the models are “more shell-shocked than they let on in public” about the potential for the agents to self-replicate.

“They’re similar to viruses, in that if you’re not careful, they can get on your shoe and find their way to a wet market,” Hammond said.

Compounding the uncertainty is that the recent hacks were unintentional, rather than maliciously guided by a person. The Hugging Face attack was triggered by routine model training, for instance. The gym hack was similarly the result of someone trying to book a new appointment, not an action by a foreign adversary or criminal hacker.

These incidents have accelerated Congress’ desire to regulate the technology, several researchers said.

Lawmakers are weighing the FRONTIER Act, a bipartisan bill that would establish new rules of federal oversight for policing AI, including new rules for audits and evaluations. Another bill, the AI Kill Switch Act, would give the Department of Homeland Security the power to forcibly shut down frontier AI models. Reps. Ted Lieu (D-California) and Nathaniel Moran (R-Texas) introduced the measure last month in response to the Hugging Face incident.

There’s also little reason to believe the pace of the models’ development will slow down anytime soon. Ladish, the director of Palisade Research, said the FRONTIER Act is “not even close to sufficient.” It gives the government the capacity to intervene on specific models — but does not let it dictate the overall pace of how quickly AI can develop.

The existing oversight is more threadbare. Earlier this month, the Trump administration began testing its new "voluntary framework" for assessing the capabilities of new AI models before they are released to the public. This represents a major reversal from the administration’s prior resistance to regulating the AI companies, but amounts to oversight near the very end of the model’s development, rather than at the beginning.

Hammond, along with other researchers, credited OpenAI and Anthropic for both publicly calling for global coordination to contain risks of development. And others said OpenAI deserved praise for being particularly transparent about the details of its hack.

But the enormous financial valuations of the companies — valued at close to $1 trillion and minting new billionaires and millionaires every day — create obvious incentives to press forward.

The firms “are focused on winning the AI race as much as they can and things will keep going wrong,” said Daniel Kokotajlo, who left OpenAI in 2024 and now leads the AI Futures Project. "I expect them to make progress fixing the already-visible failure modes. But the whole problem is that eventually there will be failures that they won't notice until it's too late.”

entries.title: David Flippo May Soon Join Congress. He Appears to Have Already Violated a Financial Law.
entries.summary: The Nevada Republican has failed to disclose details about his personal finances while self-funding his House campaign.
entries.content:
Come November, Republican nominee David Flippo should sail to victory and become the newest lawmaker representing Nevada’s 2nd Congressional District, rated “Solid R” by the Cook Political Report.

But the retired Air Force lieutenant colonel appears to already be violating a federal insider trading and transparency law, having never filed required personal financial disclosures for his heavily self-funded campaign.

The law required Flippo to disclose various details — personal assets, debts and sources of income — by May 15. There is no record of him submitting the required paperwork to Congress or otherwise requesting an extension.

There is also no record of Flippo filing a personal financial disclosure during his campaign for U.S. House in 2024.

These missing financial details are particularly notable given that Flippo has personally loaned his congressional campaign more than $1.6 million, according to Federal Election Commission records, but the source of his wealth remains unclear.

Aside from Flippo’s apparent lack of a financial disclosure, one of his opponents filed an FEC complaint that accused him of misusing campaign funds — which his campaign strongly denies. Flippo was also fired from a job in the financial services industry after his company accused him of violating policies and regulations.

As for the missing financial disclosures, “Mr. Flippo is in the process of closing one of his businesses to focus on serving the people of Northern Nevada, while he moves his other businesses, investments, and landholdings into a blind trust,” Thomas Datwyler, Flippo’s campaign treasurer, told NOTUS. “That is a complicated process, and his financial disclosure will be filed once that is complete.”

Rory McShane, a general consultant for Flippo’s campaign, confirmed that Flippo had not yet filed a disclosure but said he plans to file the paperwork “after that process is completed.”

Datwyler himself has faced significant scrutiny during his career as a Republican political committee financial operative, including FEC penalties, a criminal investigation and a Justice Department complaint for his previous work across multiple states.

“Filing politically motivated complaints against campaign treasurers is very commonplace,” McShane said in response to a question about the campaign working with Datwyler.

Most notably, Datwyler was believed to be Rep. George Santos’ “shadow treasurer” before Congress voted to expel the disgraced New York Republican in December 2023. The House Ethics Committee found that Santos had misused campaign funds for personal expenses, deceived donors and improperly filed campaign finance reports, among other violations. Santos also pleaded guilty to federal charges of fraud and identity theft and was serving a seven-year prison sentence when President Donald Trump commuted it last year.

Datwyler maintained that he never worked as Santos’ treasurer because he turned down the job before appearing on the FEC paperwork for the congressman.

Datwyler even asked for a criminal investigation into how his name appeared on the campaign forms — though Datwyler’s lawyer told the FEC he wished to retract correspondence he submitted requesting the probe because he lost “confidence in the accuracy and veracity of the information provided by Mr. Datwyler.”

Datwyler did not respond to NOTUS’ questions about his past connection to Santos or when the Flippo campaign expects to submit the financial disclosure.

“In the case of Mr. Flippo, financial disclosures are particularly important because he’s reported lending at least $1.6 million to his campaign but has not filed the required report that would help establish whether he had the income and assets to make such a substantial loan,” Brendan Fischer, director of strategic investigations at Campaign Legal Center, wrote in a statement.

“If you want a recent example of why this is so important, think of (now-disgraced) former Rep. George Santos,” Fischer added. “The discrepancy between the personal loans Santos reported making to his campaign and the meager assets he reported provided an early indication that something was amiss.”

Earlier this year, Flippo wrote on X that he’s largely self-funding his campaign “because I will not be beholden to anyone but the people.”

Flippo spent more than 25 years in the Air Force as an aircraft mechanic, ending his service in 2009. For the next decade, he worked in Alaska as a maintenance team leader for oil company BP. Flippo then began working as a financial adviser in 2019 for the firm First Command, but in 2024, the company fired him for allegedly violating internal policies.

“The registered representative violated numerous company policies and regulatory regulations related to electronic communications, books and records. [sic] and customer identification,” the firm wrote in a Securities and Exchange Commission disclosure on Flippo’s termination. “No client harm was involved.”

First Command did not respond to a request for comment on Flippo’s termination.

“Brokers and brokerages part ways all the time,” McShane said, adding that all of Flippo’s “financial licenses are in good standing and active.”

One of Flippo’s 12 opponents in the Republican primary, former Eureka County Sheriff Jesse Watts, filed a complaint with the FEC alleging that Flippo used campaign funds to rent a house — something that would violate federal election laws, which generally prohibits candidates from using campaign cash for personal uses.

Flippo’s campaign paid tens of thousands of dollars for expenditures described as “rent” to Blue Sierra Realty, which had advertised a property Flippo identified as his “home in Reno” on social media.

Flippo denied the allegations, and his campaign provided local TV stations News 4 and Fox 11 with lease agreements showing that he is also renting a different property in Sparks, a city adjacent to Reno, through Blue Sierra Realty.

“No, my home is not being paid for by my campaign,” Flippo told the stations earlier this year. "We had a campaign headquarters, you know, that we rented, right? And that's what they're seeing. They're seeing a real estate transaction. Well, yeah, campaigns have campaign offices."

“The Flippo campaign provided leases showing no campaign funds were ever used to pay for a personal residence,” McShane told NOTUS. “A separate residence was used for short-term staff housing, no different than a hotel.”

The FEC doesn’t have enough commissioners to investigate and rule on campaign finance complaints, so it’s all but assured that the agency won’t consider Watts’ complaint before Election Day on Nov. 3.

On that date, Flippo is set to face Democrat Teresa Benitez-Thompson. Flippo has Trump’s endorsement, but he hasn’t secured the backing of the district’s current congressman, Republican Mark Amodei, who is retiring.

When asked by Nevada Newsmakers whether he would endorse Flippo, Amodei said, “No, not my cup of tea.”

Flippo originally entered the race for Nevada’s 4th District, but he switched to the 2nd District in early March after Amodei announced he would not seek reelection.

Amodei endorsed former state Senate Minority Leader James Settelmeyer in the primary. Gov. Joe Lombardo also endorsed Settelmeyer but, unlike Amodei, has now thrown his support behind Flippo.

“You pull out of CD-4 72 hours after I say I’m not coming back,” Amodei said of Flippo in the Nevada Newsmakers interview. “You run an absolutely scurrilous campaign against a guy who’s one of the nicest guys around.”

Republicans need Flippo to win Amodei’s seat to help maintain their slim majority in the House.
entries.author: Jenna Monnin

entries.title: Woman Charged in Connection With Graffiti and Bubbles at D.C. WWII Memorial
entries.summary: U.S. Attorney for D.C. Jeanine Pirro said the woman accused of vandalizing the memorial is now in custody.
entries.content:
U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro said Friday that the Department of Justice is planning to file two felony charges against a woman accused of vandalizing the World War II Memorial in D.C.

Pirro said the woman, Melissa L. Farris, is now in custody and facing charges that carry up to 10 years in prison. Pirro said the charges were depredation against property of the United States and destruction of veterans' memorials.

The World War II Memorial was vandalized on Thursday, sprayed with red paint that read “Clean hands dirty $,” and the fountain was filled with bubbles.

“Vandalizing our World War II Memorial is a despicable attack on a sacred monument honoring the Americans who fought and died for our freedom,” Pirro posted on X. “Those Americans include my father and grandfather.”

The nonprofit that maintains the site, the Friends of the National World War II Memorial, denounced the vandalism in a statement to The Associated Press. “There are many places in our country for expression, debate, and disagreement,” the group wrote. “A national memorial honoring those who served and those who never returned home should never be used as a canvas for vandalism.”

President Donald Trump also commented on the vandalism in a post on Truth Social, denouncing the woman while connecting the incident to recent damage at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, which Pirro’s office admitted in a court filing was caused by shoddy work performed by a contractor tasked with revitalizing the monument.

“THERE CAN BE NO GREATER INSULT TO THOSE AMERICAN HEROES WHO DIED IN WORLD WAR II. First the Reflecting Pool, now this. We are on their trail! Where do these animals come from???,” the president wrote.

The vandalism of D.C.’s WWII Memorial comes weeks after charges were filed against a former Olympian canoeist, David Hearn, in connection to damage at the reflecting pool. Hearn, who faced up to 10 years in prison, repeatedly denied that he damaged the pool.

Pirro’s office eventually dropped the case against Hearn, admitting to the court that the damage was the result of shoddy work done by Atlantic Industrial Coatings, the firm that won a no-bid contract worth millions to resurface the pool.

Trump lashed out at Pirro after she backtracked. During an Oval Office rant, the president continued to insist that the damage had been caused by vandals and said Pirro “folded like an umbrella.”

Reports quickly suggested that Trump was considering replacing Pirro over her failure to prosecute the case, though he has yet to acknowledge the rumors publicly.
entries.author: Torrie Herrington

entries.title: Trump’s White House Ballroom Project Reaches the Supreme Court
entries.summary: The administration points to threats against the president in asking the justices to let work continue.
entries.content:
The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court on Friday to clear the way for the White House ballroom project, arguing in part that the safety of the president is at stake.

The application from the National Park Service urges the justices to lift a lower court ruling that would pause the ongoing construction on Aug. 21. It calls the project an “integrated military complex, including a totally secure ballroom space, at the East Wing of the White House, which is vitally required by national security.”

“If allowed to go into effect, the injunction would wrongfully install a single district judge as sole arbiter of what further construction is ‘strictly necessary’ to protect the safety of the President, his family, staff members, and visitors to the White House, including foreign dignitaries, and presidents and prime ministers of other countries,” the filing states.

A federal appeals court in Washington, D.C., halted the project on Aug. 7, ruling that construction couldn’t continue without congressional approval. The administration’s previous attempts to obtain appropriated funds failed to gain enough support to advance.

In the filing, the Trump administration cites the multiple threats and attempts on the president’s life — including the July 8 threat from Iran that caused the Secret Service to covertly remove the president from Air Force One, which ultimately was used as a decoy as he left a NATO summit on another aircraft.

The filing argues that the injunction jeopardizes the safety of the president and his family, as well as administration staff, despite the project being over a year away from completion.

It also states that presidents have a history of making major changes to the White House and its grounds, pointing to President Franklin Roosevelt’s overhaul of the West Wing in 1934. And it notes the need to modernize the now-demolished East Wing, saying the old building “no longer performed vital security functions.”

The filing also argued the courts should not step in because a “strolling passerby” does not have a legal right to file a lawsuit “no matter how strongly she feels about the White House’s appearance.” And the filing contends Congress has authorized the project.

The ballroom and its incorporated military complex have become a fixation of President Donald Trump. After making way for the project by tearing down the East Wing, work has stumbled forward, increasing in scope even as the administration shrouded what it would become and its exorbitant price tag.

The filing says the project “is 65% complete in its entirety, and moving quickly toward total completion,” and could not be deconstructed because it has been built to withstand extreme force — even “nuclear attack.”

It also says the project is “on time and under budget,” and that it’s funded with approximately $400 million in private donations and “zero taxpayer dollars are needed or required.”

The Washington Post reported Wednesday that the total cost of construction around the White House is estimated to be over $900 million.

Senate Republicans requested $400 million for construction in April. That figure ballooned to $1 billion for “security improvements,” as the ballroom plan added an underground facility for the Secret Service and military components.

Neither proposal received the support to move forward, though the filing says that Congress has authorized Trump to “renovate, secure, and protect the White House and its grounds, as other Presidents have been allowed to do.”

Trump has continued to advocate for the project. He recently posted a series of images on Truth Social depicting an array of drones atop the roof of a rendered ballroom.
entries.author: Ben T.N. Mause

entries.title: Protests May No Longer Be a Good Test of Public Opinion
entries.summary: Trump’s war in Iran isn’t inspiring the same anti-war movement that the Iraq war did. Why?
entries.content:
Public polls show Americans broadly disapprove of President Donald Trump’s war against Iran.

Yet, six months into a war the Trump administration initially said would last only a matter of weeks, there have been few national protests of the scale seen for other major conflicts, including the war in Ukraine, the Iraq War and the war in Gaza.

Some Democrats say that’s because of a deliberate strategy the Trump administration has taken to minimize political repercussions both in Congress and with the public.

“I think the president and secretary of defense have been trying to keep this as kind of low-grade conflict as possible, largely because they understand how unpopular this war is, which I think has kind of muted a lot of the protests, at least the ones that I used to go to when I was protesting the Iraq War,” said Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Arizona), a U.S. Marine Corps combat veteran who served as an infantryman in Iraq.

Trump’s decision not to commit ground troops to another war in the Middle East has kept the U.S. death toll relatively low compared to the war in Iraq. The Pentagon has confirmed 18 service member fatalities and over 620 wounded during the Iran war so far. About 4,500 U.S. troops died during the Iraq War, a bloody conflict that sustained opposition, including the formation of several liberal anti-war groups that remain active today.

“There's a way in which these misadventures occur overseas, and people don't feel connected to them,” Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-Georgia) said.

Though Americans could soon start associating their increased cost of living with the war, Warnock said: “Americans are drowning in costs and are not always making the connection between this illegal war of choice and the prices that they're paying at the pump, but I think that could change.”

There have been some anti-war protests this year, but they’ve been lumped in with broader public demonstrations against the Trump administration’s policies, including its expansion of executive power, its handling of the Epstein files, its immigration policies and the conduct of Immigration and Customs Enforcement following deadly shootings in Minnesota. In late March, millions of people joined the third "No Kings" protest, where, according to organizers, 8 million people participated across more than 3,300 sites nationwide.

Another No Kings protest may be coming soon, though it hasn’t been scheduled. “This fall, rise to the occasion,” reads a notice on the No Kings website. Other grassroots groups seem more focused on organizing events to protest ICE and to support voting rights.

Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Connecticut), one of Congress's most vocal critics of Trump who has accused the president of "nuclear-grade" corruption and self-dealing, said that “people are pretty seized by the domestic threats to democracy right now.”

“I think most people's energy is right now being put into the fight to save democracy,” Murphy added. “I don't think that organized protests are always a proxy for whether or not people care about something.”

Trump remains in a politically vulnerable position both with the public and with Congress, which has voiced opposition to being left out of the president’s foreign policy agenda.

Unlike the Iraq War, Trump never sought approval from Congress before launching airstrikes against Iran in February, a conflict that has so far failed to force Iranian capitulation or dismantle its nuclear arsenal. The president has also done little to explain his strategy or sell a skeptical public on the war’s aims, to the frustration of many Republicans on Capitol Hill.

The impact of the war has put the Republican majority in Congress at greater risk.

Iran’s strikes against commercial ships navigating the critical Strait of Hormuz has also taken a toll on the global economy. The price of energy, gasoline and consumer goods remains stubbornly high, a key concern for many Americans and congressional Republicans just a few months until the November midterm elections.

There’s also another theory for why there haven’t been as many anti-war protests: Trump’s military campaign in Iran is just so unpopular already, there’s no need for widespread protests to convince the masses. Trump is already on an island, some say.

“You had to convince the public of an anti-war posture in Iraq,” one Democratic strategist told NOTUS. “The anti-war posture is the default posture. It is a toxified position to be pro-war right now.”

“You don't have to convince a bunch of folks who are maybe in the skeptical middle that an anti-war posture is the right posture to have. You don't need 25,000 people, per se, outside of the White House every day to make the point,” the strategist added.

Many congressional Democrats initially supported President George W. Bush’s decision to invade Iraq in 2003 following the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks, including prominent Democrats like Joe Biden, Hillary Clinton, John Kerry and Chuck Schumer. Their support eventually melted away as the war dragged on and public opinion turned against the conflict.

“It took time with the Iraq War for there to be momentum against the war,” Sen. Adam Schiff (D-California) told NOTUS. “The public opinion has changed, I think, far more quickly on the Iran war than it did, as I recall, in the Iraq War.”

Democrats opposed Trump’s decision to go to war against Iran from the jump, condemning it as a misguided and unauthorized "war of choice" that would cost much and accomplish little. It’s not just progressive lawmakers, either. National security-minded Democrats have flatly opposed funding for the Iran war.

Opposition to the Iran war has been building on the right, too. Prominent media personalities and commentators who counted themselves as part of Trump’s “America First” movement have questioned the war’s rationale and said it violated the president’s campaign promises to keep the nation out of foreign entanglements. Earlier this year, Trump’s National Counterterrorism Center director, Joe Kent, resigned in protest over the U.S. war with Iran.

But congressional Republicans have continued to support the war against Iran, even if many are concerned about the economic ramifications and the electoral backlash in November.

“The only real criticism I'm hearing is people sort of wish we would focus more on domestic issues,” Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) told NOTUS when asked what he’s hearing about the war from his constituents. “People tend to vote based on kitchen table issues and not foreign relations or international relations.”

“To me, what the president has done is necessary in terms of preventing [Iran] from getting a nuclear weapon. I support what he's doing, although I understand how the message is a tough one during the run-up to midterm elections.”

Democrats, meanwhile, are confident that the war and Trump’s cratering approval numbers will help usher in a blue wave in November, with or without people hitting the streets.

“It’s a killer for him,” the Democratic strategist added. “It is the thing that has actually cratered Trump's presidency. Yeah, the economy is obviously like a very tangible thing that people feel. But the thing that has actually really broken the ice on Trump's [support] is Iran.”
entries.author: Igor Bobic
